coverage.note: The Microsoft function inventory contains 521 entries. One hundred fifteen functions are conformance-tested with shared Python/Rust fixtures; the remaining 406 of the 521 inventoried functions are catalog-only. Criteria functions implement scalar criteria, comparison operators, case-insensitive text, wildcard escapes, and bounded range shapes. SUMIF and AVERAGEIF reject differently sized sum/average ranges even though Excel aligns those ranges from their top-left cell; that compatibility gap is explicit in semantic_specs. MINIFS and MAXIFS require matching range shapes, allow one required plus up to 126 additional criteria pairs, and return 0 when no numeric result matches. XLOOKUP and XMATCH support exact match_mode=0 with forward/reverse search_mode=1/-1 only; approximate, wildcard, binary, and array-spill results are unsupported. TEXTBEFORE and TEXTAFTER support scalar delimiter extraction, optional arguments, negative instance numbers, match_end, and lazy if_not_found; their Excel locale collation and supplementary-plane character behavior remain unverified. ISNA, ISERR, ISERROR, and NA cover scalar inspection and creation of supported Excel error values; array error predicates and unsupported-syntax conversions remain out of scope. INT, TRUNC, ROUNDUP, ROUNDDOWN, MOD, and QUOTIENT add scalar directed rounding, floor/truncation, remainder, and integer-quotient behavior. Fractional num_digits values are truncated toward zero as an implementation rule; Microsoft pages do not specify this case, and direct Excel spot-checks remain outstanding. MONTH, DAYS, EDATE, and EOMONTH use the 1900 serial system and preserve its serial-60 compatibility date; DAYS subtracts numeric serials including their fractional parts. EDATE and EOMONTH truncate fractional month counts toward zero; both month-shift functions return whole-day serials, and EDATE discards a start serial's time fraction as an implementation profile rule. Locale-dependent text-date parsing and workbook-specific 1904 date systems are not modeled; time-fraction handling for EDATE/EOMONTH has not been spot-checked in Excel. HOUR, MINUTE, and SECOND extract whole-second components from numeric 1900-system serials; the serial ceiling and negative/non-finite input errors are evaluator profile rules not stated on the function pages. Locale-dependent time text such as '6:45 PM' is documented by Microsoft but not parsed here. The shared serial-to-seconds precision correction and TIME fractional-component truncation are evaluator profile rules that need Excel spot-checks. TIME accepts components from 0 through 32767, normalizes overflow, and returns a fraction of a day. IFS and SWITCH use ordered short-circuit evaluation and first-match selection; selected results may preserve a rectangular array through evaluate_result, but are not projected into worksheet cells. SWITCH treats ASCII text as case-insensitive and non-ASCII text as exact, with no cross-type coercion or locale collation. Microsoft documents selection/default behavior but not all evaluation and comparison details; these evaluator profile rules need a direct Excel spot-check. WEEKDAY, WEEKNUM, and ISOWEEKNUM add numeric 1900-system date serials, documented return selectors, System 1 and ISO week rules, and time-fraction flooring. Fractional return_type coercion and exact 1900 serial-60 week behavior are evaluator-profile rules that still need Excel spot-checks. WORKDAY and NETWORKDAYS use a Saturday/Sunday business calendar and scalar or cell-range holidays. NETWORKDAYS counts weekday endpoints inclusively; reversed-range sign, fractional date serials, holiday-cell coercion, serial 0, and serial 60 are explicit evaluator profiles that still need direct Excel spot-checks. WORKDAY truncates noninteger day offsets as Microsoft documents; holiday-cell coercion remains unverified. WORKDAY.INTL and NETWORKDAYS.INTL share numeric weekend codes, Monday-first seven-character masks, and range-based holiday handling. NETWORKDAYS.INTL documents inclusive and reversed-range counts plus zero for an all-one weekend mask. Its last example prose says 22 while the result column says 20 for mask 0010001 with holidays; fixtures follow the result column; WORKDAY.INTL documents zero-offset behavior and rejects the all-one mask, but its exact error is unspecified. Numeric selector coercion, date fractions, serial boundaries, and holiday-cell coercion remain profiles; holiday array constants and locale-sensitive date text are not implemented. DAYS360 and YEARFRAC add a bounded 30/360 and year-fraction slice. The published DAYS360 rules cover US NASD and European methods and negative direction; non-month-end US endpoint wording, numeric and blank-cell method handling, optional-slot parsing, fractional date serials, and serial 60 remain evaluator profiles. YEARFRAC covers bases 0-4, documented integer truncation and error codes, and Microsoft examples. Basis 1 uses a year-segmented Actual/Actual profile and reversed dates use a signed result; Microsoft does not specify those details on its function page, so neither is claimed as verified Excel behavior. The 1900 date system and serial 60 remain explicit evaluator profiles. The six COUP schedule formulas share a maturity-anchored, backward-stepped date schedule in the evaluator and expose separate function-specific outputs. Microsoft documents argument truncation, valid frequencies 1/2/4, basis values 0-4, output definitions, and date/frequency/basis/order errors. The maturity-anchored schedule, period/count equality behavior outside the documented strict COUPNCD/COUPPCD boundaries, basis-specific day counts, serial-60 behavior, and pre-zero internal coupon dates remain evaluator profiles. COUPDAYS basis 1 uses actual adjacent coupon-date serial difference but has not been checked against Excel; ExcelFinancialFunctions compatibility notes identify leap-year COUPDAYS differences, so shared expected values are not treated as Excel oracles. FV, PV, and PMT add a scalar periodic-cash-flow slice with shared sign, timing, zero-rate, omission, and numeric-profile cases. NPER inverts the periodic cash-flow equation, preserves negative and fractional results, and checks zero-rate and logarithm-domain boundaries under explicit evaluator profiles. Exact internal precision and undocumented input errors remain unverified. IPMT and PPMT split PMT into period interest and principal components; PPMT is defined as PMT minus IPMT, and both use explicit timing, range, numeric, and error profiles pending direct Excel checks. At accepted Run 19, the shared fixture corpus contained 1,238 cases covering 112 implemented functions, with 409 of the 521 inventory entries catalog-only. Run 20 adds elementwise binary operators and FILTER to both evaluators; SORT and UNIQUE remain source-linked catalog-only records. Its accepted checkpoint and detailed case summary follow below. SLN and SYD add straight-line and sum-of-years-digits depreciation. DB adds the documented three-decimal rate and month-sensitive first/final periods; DDB adds the documented factor-based decline and salvage cap. VDB adds fractional-interval depreciation, optional straight-line switching, and a logarithmic-time geometric kernel; its split fractional-period behavior remains an evaluator profile because an Apache compatibility note reports a difference from Excel. Their bounds, truncation, coercion, error precedence, and high-range behavior remain evaluator profiles pending direct Excel checks. Apache ExcelFinancialFunctions and dual MIT/Apache Formualizer inform organization and numeric probes only; no code is copied. The Microsoft Office formula specification distinguishes normal-formula implicit intersection from array-entered full-range behavior and lists ISEVEN/ISODD as accepting range arguments. Run 19 adds bounded rectangular result arrays and SEQUENCE, and common aggregates/text/logical consumers flatten generated arrays. IF, IFERROR, IFNA, IFS, and SWITCH also preserve the selected result-array shape. Microsoft lists worksheet number precision as 15 digits. The EVEN/ODD fixtures using 16-digit values near 2^53 are Workbook Forge binary64 parser/evaluator boundary probes, not Excel numerical oracles. Run 16 adds FACT, COMBIN, and COMBINA. The Python and Rust kernels form exact integer factorial/binomial results and round once to binary64 with ties-to-even; Apache Commons Math informs the symmetric multiplicative pattern without copied code or a runtime dependency. Within FACT, COMBIN, and COMBINA arguments, plain integer literals, unary signs, +, -, *, and nonnegative integer-power expressions preserve exact source integers through the 2^53 argument boundary, subject to a 65,536-bit intermediate cap. Exact integer division forms a ratio and rounds once to binary64; mixed or decimal operands use binary64 division. Decimal/scientific literals can round before the check. Scalar coercion, truncation-before-domain order for negative fractions, mixed-error precedence, and local #NUM! overflow behavior remain Workbook Forge profiles where Microsoft sources are silent. Standalone expression arithmetic can preserve Python integers while Rust uses binary64 operators; exact-source cross-language assertions are scoped to the three named function arguments. Range errors are kept separate from Excel implicit-intersection and array-entry behavior because the function evaluator does not model general worksheet formula context. The Python workbook adapter separately handles explicitly targeted scalar formulas and static dependencies, without implicit intersection or array entry. Run 17 adds FACTDOUBLE, PERMUT, and PERMUTATIONA with Microsoft-linked semantics and independent bounded exact-integer kernels. FACTDOUBLE is range-capable in the Office formula specification but Workbook Forge retains a scalar-only local range boundary; PERMUTATIONA 0^0, negative-input handling, coercion, output rounding, and overflow remain evaluator profiles pending direct Excel checks. No source code is copied and runtime dependencies remain empty. Run 18 adds GCD and LCM with Microsoft-linked argument, truncation, error, and 2^53 boundary rules. Both are range-capable in MS-OE376, but range calls remain a local unsupported boundary until formula-cell context is modeled. GCD(0,0), LCM zero behavior, mixed-input order, coercion, and negative-fraction order are explicitly local profiles pending Excel checks. Run 19 adds SEQUENCE with an immutable rectangular ArrayValue and shape-preserving evaluate_result API in Python and Rust. Thirty-eight shared cases cover Microsoft’s 4×5 shape example, row-major progression, optional slots, ranges, nested SUM, dimension/coercion/error profiles and the 100000-cell local cap. FILTER, SORT and UNIQUE have source-linked catalog-only semantics; selection, sort comparison, uniqueness comparison and spill behavior remain unimplemented. Formualizer v0.7.0 informs the separation between pre-allocation shape bounds and workbook spill projection; its MIT/Apache-2.0 release is an architecture reference only and no code was copied. No direct Excel spot-checks were run.. Run 20 adds elementwise binary operators and FILTER to the bounded array result layer. The accepted slice has 113 functions with shared Python/Rust fixture parity, 1,301 shared fixtures, 84 detailed specs, 107 source records, 16 OSS patterns, and 408 catalog-only inventory functions. Sixty-three new shared cases cover all advertised binary operators, exact-shape pairing, scalar broadcasting, cell errors, Microsoft's AND/OR include-mask examples, vertical and horizontal FILTER masks, fallback behavior, comparison-coercion and error-precedence profiles, and shape/error boundaries. Numeric, blank, and empty-text mask coercion; explicit missing fallback; row-major mask error order; lazy fallback; array-valued fallback shape; and binary comparison collation/coercion and left-to-right binary-operator error precedence are Workbook Forge profiles. semantics.definition: Returns prorated accounting-period depreciation using a life-dependent coefficient under the French depreciation method. Microsoft currently marks the function deprecated and retained for old-workbook compatibility.
semantics.day_count_basis: Microsoft documents basis 0 or omitted as US/NASD 30/360, 1 as actual, 3 as actual/365, and 4 as European 30/360. Excel truncates basis to an integer and Office uses only 0, 1, 3, or 4; basis 2 is excluded.
semantics.coefficient_profile: Microsoft lists coefficient 1.5 for useful lives between 3 and 4, 2 for 5 and 6, and 2.5 above 6. The evaluator uses ceil(1/rate) before coefficient selection, following ExcelFinancialFunctions. It rejects raw useful lives <=3 and 4<=life<=5 as an evaluator profile resolving ambiguous overlapping Microsoft ranges; Apache OpenOffice uses different band selection and is retained as a comparison only.
semantics.equation_profile: Evaluator profile informed by ExcelFinancialFunctions: multiply rate by the life coefficient; prorate period 0 using the selected day-count fraction and round to whole currency units. When the original unrounded stub is exactly zero, substitute cost times the effective rate for period 0 and keep the base life. A positive stub adds one schedule step. Later periods use the remaining book value and the effective declining rate, switching to half of remaining book value when two schedule steps remain and to the full remaining book value on the following step. Period inputs after ceil(1/rate) still return zero. If book value is already below salvage, the later-period amount is zero. The calculation does not clamp every amount to remaining book value minus salvage, so a rounded step can carry the book value below salvage. These are reference-derived evaluator behaviors, not a general Microsoft-published equation or an Excel-verified claim.
semantics.period_index_profile: Evaluator profile: period 0 is the prorated stub and period 1 is the first post-stub depreciation amount. Microsoft documents a period-1 example of 776 but does not define the complete index schedule.
semantics.date_profile: Dates are numeric 1900-system Excel serials; fractional serials truncate toward zero to calendar days, locale text dates are unsupported, and purchase must precede first_period. Day-count leap-day handling follows the local serial calendar; exact Excel behavior remains unverified. Basis 1 uses denominator 366 only when the inclusive serial interval contains February 29, otherwise 365; serial 60 is treated as the shared 1900-system compatibility date 1900-02-29.
semantics.input_profile: Arguments use shared scalar numeric coercion. Cost must be positive, 0<=salvage<cost, rate positive and finite, and period truncates toward zero to 0..100000. Useful-life and period ceilings, allowed basis values, date bounds/order, and error codes are evaluator profiles where Excel is silent or ambiguous.
semantics.compatibility_notes: ExcelFinancialFunctions documents an Excel-compatible rounding switch for an edge case whose outputs differ by one unit; its ordinary path and Apache OpenOffice also differ in coefficient bands/validation. The evaluator uses half-up period rounding, the ceil-life coefficient profile, and the zero-stub full-year fallback. Shared cases include Microsoft’s displayed 776 example plus independent derivations/reference-derived cases; they do not establish Excel compatibility. No code is copied.

derived_examples.basis: 134/365 stub fraction times cost 2400 and effective 37.5% rate, rounded half-up because the interval contains no February 29; implementation-derived, not a Microsoft-published result.
A 3.5-year raw life selects coefficient 1.5; the full-period basis-3 stub is 1000*(2/7)*1.5, rounded half-up. Period 0; reference-derived, not Excel-checked.
A 5.5-year raw life selects coefficient 2; the full-period basis-3 stub is rounded half-up. Period 0; reference-derived, not Excel-checked.
A 6.5-year raw life selects coefficient 2.5; the full-period basis-3 stub is rounded half-up. Period 0; reference-derived, not Excel-checked.
The local NASD 30/360 helper yields 183/360 days; applying the 37.5% effective rate and half-up rounding. Reference/profile-derived, not Excel-checked.
The NASD 30/360 stub is zero, so the reference-derived evaluator profile uses cost*(2/7)*1.5 for period 0; half-up rounding gives 429. Not a Microsoft-published result.

semantics.rounding_profile: The period-0 amount and later period amounts are rounded half-up to whole currency units. If the prorated stub is exactly zero, the reference-derived evaluator profile substitutes the full-year effective-rate amount for period 0 and keeps the base life; a positive unrounded stub adds one schedule step. Because later amounts are not clamped to remaining book value minus salvage, cumulative depreciation can cross below salvage; subsequent periods return zero once book value is below salvage. This profile is informed by ExcelFinancialFunctions and is not directly checked against Excel.

semantics.definition: Returns depreciation for an accounting period under the French linear depreciation method, including prorated depreciation for an asset purchased during an accounting period.
semantics.day_count_basis: Microsoft documents basis 0 or omitted as US/NASD 30/360, 1 as actual, 3 as actual/365, and 4 as European 30/360. The Microsoft Excel Open Specification says Excel truncates basis to an integer and uses only 0, 1, 3, or 4; basis 2 is not used by Office. For basis 1, the evaluator uses 366 only when the inclusive serial interval contains February 29 (including compatibility serial 60); otherwise it uses 365.
semantics.equation_profile: Evaluator profile informed by the Apache-2.0 ExcelFinancialFunctions reference: period 0 normally returns min(cost*rate*stub_year_fraction, cost-salvage); when the unrounded stub is exactly zero, it substitutes min(cost*rate, cost-salvage). Later periods return min(cost*rate, remaining depreciable basis after period 0 and prior full annual amounts). The Excel function page does not publish a general equation.
semantics.period_index_profile: Evaluator profile: period 0 represents the prorated stub, period 1 is the first full annual amount. Microsoft documents a period-1 result of 360 for its 2400 cost and 15% rate example but does not define general period indexing; the reference implementation uses this zero-based stub convention.
semantics.date_profile: Dates are numeric 1900-system Excel serials; fractional serials are truncated toward zero to calendar days, text-date parsing is unsupported, and the purchase date must precede the first-period date. The date range and purchase-order restriction are evaluator profiles. Basis 1 uses a 366-day denominator only when the inclusive interval contains February 29; otherwise its denominator is 365. Serial 60 is treated as the shared 1900-system compatibility date 1900-02-29.
semantics.input_profile: Arguments use shared scalar numeric coercion. Cost must be positive, 0<=salvage<cost, rate must be positive and finite, and period truncates toward zero to an integer from 0 through 100000. The reciprocal rate must be finite and its ceiling must not exceed 9,007,199,254,740,991. Domain bounds, period truncation/cap, date handling, and error codes are evaluator profiles where Microsoft is silent.
semantics.rounding_profile: AMORLINC retains fractional currency amounts; no per-period whole-unit rounding is applied by this evaluator. This is an evaluator profile, not a direct Excel check.
semantics.source_example_issue: The Microsoft Excel page data table puts the rate in A7 and basis 1 in A8, but the displayed formula passes A7 as both rate and basis. The Microsoft Open Specification says basis is truncated, so 0.15 selects basis 0, not the stated Actual basis 1. The separate DAX example uses a literal basis 1 but is not normative for Excel; both examples return 360, which does not distinguish the bases.
semantics.compatibility_notes: ExcelFinancialFunctions supplies the period-0 stub interpretation, the zero-stub full-year fallback, and test-data organization. These are implementation references only; no source code is copied. Direct Excel checks are still needed for period indexing, period 0, fractional periods, leap dates, the zero-stub fallback, and undocumented invalid inputs.

derived_examples.basis: Actual/Actual day fraction 134/365 times cost 2400 and rate 0.15 because this interval contains no February 29; reference-derived, not a Microsoft-published result.
The NASD 30/360 stub is zero; the reference-derived evaluator profile falls back to cost*rate, capped at cost-salvage. Not a Microsoft-published result.

semantics.definition: Returns the number of unordered selections of number_chosen items from number distinct items, C(n,k).
semantics.documented_behavior: Microsoft documents truncation of numeric arguments, #VALUE! for nonnumeric arguments, #NUM! when either integer argument is negative or number is less than number_chosen, and COMBIN(8,2)=28.
semantics.truncation_and_domain_profile: Workbook Forge truncates arguments toward zero before checking the resulting integer domain. Microsoft documents truncation and domain constraints but does not specify their order for negative fractional values; direct Excel spot-checking is still needed.
semantics.implementation: The evaluator uses k = min(k, n-k), forms the exact integer coefficient with a bounded multiplicative recurrence, then rounds once to binary64; this avoids factorial intermediates and cross-runtime rounding drift.
semantics.coercion_profile: Workbook Forge applies its shared scalar numeric coercer: blank values, Boolean values, empty text, and ASCII numeric text are converted to numbers; nonnumeric text returns #VALUE! and existing formula errors propagate. Range rejection takes precedence, then the first existing formula error in argument order; if no formula error exists, scalar coercion proceeds left to right. Function-specific numeric-domain validation occurs after all scalar coercions succeed. For multi-argument combinatorics functions, a later invalid text argument returns #VALUE! before an earlier negative count produces #NUM!; this is an unverified Workbook Forge mixed-input profile. Microsoft does not specify these mixed-error precedence rules or subtype coercions.
semantics.range_behavior: MS-OE376 §3.17.2 lists the range-capable function arguments and does not list this function (FACTDOUBLE is listed). Normal formulas therefore use Office implicit intersection when possible; array-entered formulas receive full ranges. Workbook Forge has no formula-cell or array-entry context and returns #VALUE! for a range argument as a local scalar boundary, not as an Excel expected result.
semantics.numeric_profile: Workbook Forge uses finite binary64 scalar values and accepts integer arguments only through 2^53; larger magnitudes are rejected because adjacent integers are no longer all exactly representable. Within FACT, FACTDOUBLE, COMBIN, COMBINA, PERMUT, and PERMUTATIONA argument expressions, plain integer literals, unary signs, +, -, *, and nonnegative integer-power expressions preserve exact source integers through the boundary check, subject to a 65,536-bit intermediate cap. Exact integer division forms a ratio and rounds once to binary64; mixed or decimal operands use binary64 division. Decimal/scientific literals also follow binary64 parsing and may round before the check. The exact integer coefficient is rounded once to binary64 using round-to-nearest, ties-to-even. A result outside the finite binary64 range returns #NUM! as a local profile. Microsoft documents 15-digit worksheet precision and a largest formula result near 1.7976931348623158e+308, but does not specify the exact overflow error for this function. No direct Excel spot-check has been performed.

semantics.definition: Counts days from the prior coupon date to settlement. Bases 0 and 4 use their corresponding 30/360 day-count helpers; bases 1 through 3 use the actual serial-day difference. The detailed basis behavior is an evaluator profile.
semantics.argument_truncation: Microsoft specifies that all arguments are truncated to integers. This evaluator truncates numeric date serials, frequency, and basis toward zero before their range checks.
semantics.invalid_inputs: Microsoft documents #VALUE! for invalid settlement or maturity dates, #NUM! for frequency outside 1, 2, or 4, #NUM! for basis outside 0 through 4, and #NUM! when settlement is on or after maturity.
semantics.date_schedule_profile: The evaluator anchors coupon dates to maturity and steps backward by 12/frequency months. It preserves month-end when maturity is month-end; otherwise it preserves the maturity day and clamps shorter months. Microsoft does not specify these schedule-generation details on the function pages.
semantics.coupon_boundary_profile: Microsoft defines COUPNCD as the next coupon date after settlement and COUPPCD as the previous coupon date before settlement; the evaluator applies those strict comparisons, so exact coupon-date equality selects the following and preceding scheduled dates, respectively. The evaluator treats settlement on a coupon date as period start for COUPDAYBS, COUPDAYS, and COUPDAYSNC, and counts COUPNUM dates strictly after settlement (including maturity); these period/count equality rules and the maturity-anchored schedule remain profiles requiring direct Excel spot-checks.
semantics.basis_date_schedule_profile: The evaluator uses the same coupon schedule for all basis values. Microsoft documents basis names and mappings but does not specify whether basis changes coupon dates or coupon count.
semantics.fractional_serial_profile: All four arguments are truncated toward zero, following Microsoft. Locale-dependent date text is not parsed; numeric-text coercion and fractional serial boundaries have not been spot-checked in Excel.
semantics.serial_range: User-supplied date serials are restricted to 0 through 2958465; invalid dates return #VALUE! as Microsoft documents. Prior internal coupon dates before serial zero can be represented as negative output serials, an unverified evaluator profile.
semantics.serial_60: Preserves serial 60 as the evaluator date 1900-02-29. Coupon schedule and basis behavior around this compatibility date are unverified.
semantics.date_system: Assumes Excel 1900 date system; workbook-specific 1904 date settings are not modeled.
semantics.error_precedence_profile: When multiple inputs are invalid, this evaluator validates settlement, maturity, frequency, basis, then settlement-before-maturity. Microsoft does not specify error precedence.

semantics.equation_profile: Let L=log1p(rate) and D=-expm1(-nper*L). For end-timed periods first..last, let m=last-first+1 and z=(first-1-nper)*L+log_exprel(m*L)+log(L/rate), where log_exprel(x)=log(expm1(x)/x); then delta=-m*expm1(z) and CUMIPMT=-pv*rate*delta/D. For beginning timing, omit period 1 and divide the end-timed interest sum by 1+rate. The exact identity is CUMPRINC=selected_period_count*PMT(rate,nper,pv,0,type)-CUMIPMT, but the evaluator sums principal directly to avoid cancellation. Let L=log1p(rate) and D=1-exp(-nper*L). For an end-timed range ending at last with count selected periods, its principal log magnitude is log(pv)+(last-nper)*L+log1mexp(count*L)-log1mexp(nper*L), where log1mexp(x)=log(1-exp(-x)); negate the exponential of this value. For beginning timing, omit period 1 from that geometric principal range, divide it by 1+rate, and add the first PMT_due if selected. When nper*rate<1e-12, use the average-balance interest limit and zero-rate principal limit -pv*selected_period_count/nper. The range evaluation is O(1), with no period-by-period loop.

semantics.end_period_profile: end_period greater than nper returns #NUM! in this evaluator, following the Apache reference range guard. Microsoft does not state this boundary on the function page.

semantics.coercion_profile: Workbook Forge applies its shared scalar numeric coercer: blank values, Boolean values, empty text, and ASCII numeric text are converted to numbers; nonnumeric text returns #VALUE! and existing formula errors propagate. Range rejection takes precedence, then the first existing formula error in argument order; if no formula error exists, scalar coercion proceeds left to right. Function-specific numeric-domain validation occurs after all scalar coercions succeed. For multi-argument combinatorics functions, a later invalid text argument returns #VALUE! before an earlier negative count produces #NUM!; this is an unverified Workbook Forge mixed-input profile. Microsoft does not specify these mixed-error precedence rules or subtype coercions.
semantics.range_behavior: MS-OE376 §3.17.2 lists the range-capable function arguments and does not list this function (FACTDOUBLE is listed). Normal formulas therefore use Office implicit intersection when possible; array-entered formulas receive full ranges. Workbook Forge has no formula-cell or array-entry context and returns #VALUE! for a range argument as a local scalar boundary, not as an Excel expected result.
semantics.numeric_profile: Workbook Forge uses finite binary64 scalar values and accepts integer arguments only through 2^53; larger magnitudes are rejected because adjacent integers are no longer all exactly representable. A result outside the finite binary64 range returns #NUM! as a local profile. semantics.definition: Calculates the constant periodic payment for a loan or investment at a constant rate; it includes principal and interest but not taxes, reserves, or fees.
semantics.equation_profile: For rate != 0, PMT = -(pv + fv/(1+rate)^nper) / ((1+rate*type)*(1-(1+rate)^(-nper))/rate); for rate = 0, PMT = -(pv+fv)/nper. The stable evaluator uses equivalent log1p/expm1 expressions.
semantics.optional_slots: fv defaults to zero. type defaults to zero.
semantics.rate_period: rate is the interest rate per payment period; nper counts payment periods using the same interval. Annual rates must be converted to the payment interval, as Microsoft documents.
semantics.payment_timing: type=0 or omitted means payments at each period end; type=1 means payments at each period beginning, as Microsoft documents.
semantics.cash_flow_sign: Cash paid out is negative and cash received is positive, as Microsoft documents for annuity functions.
semantics.calculation_profile: The evaluator uses log1p/expm1-based periodic growth and annuity factors, with an exact zero-rate limit. Excel's internal numeric algorithm and precision are not specified by the cited pages.
semantics.input_profile: Arguments use the evaluator's shared numeric coercion before domain checks: blank cells, empty text, and omitted optional slots become zero; FALSE/TRUE become 0/1; and ASCII numeric text is parsed. Microsoft does not specify all of these coercions, so they are evaluator profiles. After coercion, this evaluator requires finite inputs and results, rejects rate <= -1 and negative nper with #NUM!, requires type to equal 0 or 1, evaluates fractional nper through the analytic equation, and returns #DIV/0! for PMT when the annuity factor is zero.
semantics.zero_period_profile: At nper=0, FV returns the negated present value and PV returns the negated future value; PMT returns #DIV/0! because its annuity factor is zero. Microsoft does not specify zero-period outcomes on the cited pages.
semantics.error_precedence_profile: Argument calculation errors propagate before numeric-domain validation. semantics.definition: Generates a rectangular array of sequential numbers.
semantics.documented_behavior: Microsoft documents SEQUENCE(rows,[columns],[start],[step]), says optional arguments default to 1, describes rows and columns, and states that a final array result spills into the worksheet grid.
semantics.implementation: Python and Rust independently construct the same row-major rectangular array. ArrayValue preserves shape and the public evaluate_result API returns it. IF, IFERROR, IFNA, IFS, and SWITCH preserve a selected array result. SUM, AVERAGE, COUNT, COUNTA, MIN, MAX, AND, OR, CONCAT, TEXTJOIN, and COUNTBLANK consume generated arrays through their existing flattening rules. Binary arithmetic (+, -, *, /, ^), comparisons, and concatenation also lift elementwise across equal-shaped ranges/arrays and broadcast scalar operands.
semantics.omission_profile: The engines allow omitted rows when a later argument is present and default the omitted row dimension to 1. Microsoft says an omitted rows argument requires another argument but does not show its resulting shape; this Workbook Forge choice is unverified.
semantics.dimension_profile: Both engines use the shared scalar numeric coercer, truncate dimensions toward zero, and return #NUM! for zero or negative dimensions. Microsoft’s SEQUENCE page does not specify these coercions or error codes; they are Workbook Forge profiles.
semantics.allocation_profile: Both engines reject arrays larger than 100000 cells before allocation. The cap reuses the existing evaluator range budget and is a Workbook Forge resource policy; Microsoft worksheet and array limits are larger and context-dependent.
semantics.numeric_profile: Start and step use finite binary64 values. Values follow start + row-major-index × step. Nonfinite inputs or generated outputs return #NUM! under a local Workbook Forge profile.
semantics.worksheet_boundary: ArrayValue is a computed result, not a spill projection. Workbook Forge does not place spill cells, detect blocked/merged/table destinations, model A1# or @ implicit intersection, or calculate dependency invalidation for spill regions.
semantics.compatibility_limit: Shared fixtures establish Python/Rust parity for this bounded evaluator profile; no direct Excel spot-checks have been performed.
semantics.error_precedence_profile: Arguments are evaluated left to right; the first encountered formula error or evaluation failure stops later arguments. Ordinary scalar coercion follows expression evaluation, so a later formula error can precede coercion of an earlier nonnumeric text value. A non-finite numeric literal fails when encountered. These mixed-error ordering choices are Workbook Forge profiles, not Microsoft claims.
semantics.array_operator_boundary_profile: Workbook Forge lifts binary arithmetic (+, -, *, /, ^), comparisons, and concatenation elementwise over bounded ranges and arrays. Two array operands must have exactly equal shapes; scalar operands broadcast on either side. Shape mismatches return #VALUE!, and cell-level formula errors remain in their result cells. For binary comparisons, numeric-like operands are checked before type dispatch; finite values use binary64 precision, and nonfinite/out-of-range values return #NUM!; ASCII text is case-insensitive, while text comparison is exact if either operand contains non-ASCII characters; blank, Boolean, and numeric values compare after numeric coercion; text-to-number equality is false, inequality is true, and text-to-number ordering returns #VALUE!. Binary operand errors propagate left to right: a left formula error precedes a non-finite right operand, while a non-finite left numeric operand returns #NUM! before a right formula error. This error precedence is a local Workbook Forge profile. These comparison precision, collation, and coercion rules are local Workbook Forge profiles; values beyond Excel's documented 15-digit precision are not Excel oracles. Unary operators, array constants, general broadcasting, and worksheet spill projection are not modeled. Microsoft documents elementwise array operators; this narrower shape and error profile is not a claim of complete Excel semantics.

semantics.error_profile: Formula errors propagate. Negative cost or salvage, nonpositive life, nonfinite inputs, or a nonfinite result return #NUM! as evaluator profiles. Microsoft does not specify error codes or precedence for these cases.
semantics.calculation_profile: A scalar arithmetic kernel is kept separate from domain validation. The shared Python/Rust fixtures establish the evaluator profile only; they are not direct Excel results except for the cited Microsoft example.

semantics.selector_profile: Workbook Forge accepts finite integral numeric sort_index and sort_order selectors and a Boolean by_col selector. The selected index must be within the source axis; order must be 1 or -1. Invalid selectors return #VALUE!.
semantics.comparison_profile: The selected key axis must contain one homogeneous type: finite binary64 numbers or text. Numeric keys compare as binary64. Text keys lowercase ASCII letters consistently and keep non-ASCII characters exact. Mixed types, blanks, and Booleans return #VALUE!; non-finite numeric keys return #NUM!. Selected-key errors propagate before type validation. Validation then follows key-axis order. semantics.definition: Returns depreciation over a requested interval using declining balance, with optional switching to straight-line depreciation.
semantics.equation_profile: Microsoft describes VDB as using the double-declining-balance method or another factor. Its DDB page defines each declining-balance amount as min(book_before_period*factor/life, book_before_period-salvage). The evaluator compares that amount with straight-line depreciation over the remaining life and switches at the first whole period where straight-line is greater, unless no_switch is TRUE.
semantics.interval_profile: Evaluator profile: each unit period contributes its period depreciation multiplied by the overlap length with [start_period,end_period). Fractional endpoints are prorated; the interval is evaluated directly rather than by subtracting two large cumulative totals. This profile is not asserted to match Excel for general fractional starts.
semantics.fractional_life_profile: Fractional life is accepted as an evaluator profile. The final sub-period uses the remaining fractional duration; with switching enabled the remaining basis is allocated over that tail when straight-line exceeds the capped DDB amount.
semantics.default_profile: Microsoft documents factor default 2 and says no_switch FALSE or omitted permits switching; TRUE prevents the switch. An explicitly omitted optional factor defaults to 2 even when no_switch is supplied. A blank referenced factor coerces to zero and is rejected; a blank referenced no_switch value is false as an evaluator profile.
semantics.input_profile: Arguments use shared scalar numeric coercion for cost, salvage, life, interval endpoints, and factor. Cost must be positive, 0<=salvage<=cost, life and factor must be positive, and 0<=start_period<=end_period<=life. Life is limited to 9,007,199,254,740,991 periods so whole-period arithmetic remains exact in binary64. no_switch uses the evaluator logical coercion profile: Booleans and numeric values use shared truth coercion: zero, blank, and empty text are false, any nonzero number is true, and nonempty text is rejected. These bounds and coercions are evaluator profiles; Microsoft does not fully specify them.
semantics.calculation_profile: The no-switch DDB schedule is summed as a geometric series with an explicit salvage-cap period. The switch period is found by binary search over whole periods, then the remaining straight-line interval is calculated directly. Work is O(log life), not proportional to the number of periods. Python and Rust use independent implementations. If factor/life underflows to zero, a log-space fallback preserves representable depreciation amounts.
semantics.error_profile: Formula errors propagate before numeric-domain validation. Invalid bounds, nonfinite inputs/results, and life above the exact-period limit return #NUM!; missing required arguments and invalid logical text return #VALUE!. Microsoft does not specify all error codes or precedence.
semantics.documented_conflicts: Microsoft says salvage may be 0 and publishes examples whose start_period is 0, but the same page says all arguments except no_switch must be positive. The evaluator accepts zero salvage and zero start_period based on the explicit examples and statement.
semantics.compatibility_notes: ExcelFinancialFunctions reports that Excel may return a different total for a fractional interval than for adjacent split intervals when straight-line switching is enabled. Its own implementation remains additive; this evaluator likewise defines a deterministic prorated schedule. No split-interval additivity is claimed for Excel, and the discrepancy needs a direct Excel spot-check.

independent_derived_examples.basis: DDB periods 1-3 are 40, 24, and 14.4; straight-line periods 4-5 are 10.3 each.
No-switch geometric DDB sequence is 40, 24, 14.4, 8.64, and 5.184.
The first period DDB amount is 100/13; the evaluator profile applies a 0.5-period overlap.

semantics.invalid_argument: Nonnumeric or finite out-of-range date arguments return #VALUE! in this evaluator. Microsoft documents #VALUE! for invalid date arguments; non-finite numeric values follow the separate evaluator profile.
semantics.invalid_result: A computed date outside serials 0 through 2958465 returns #NUM!, matching Microsoft documentation for invalid results.
semantics.days_bound: Offsets larger than the maximum supported date serial are rejected with #NUM! before the bounded binary search.
semantics.nonfinite_date_profile: An overflowing non-finite date expression returns #NUM! in both evaluators; the Microsoft function pages do not specify this case, and it has not been spot-checked in Excel. semantics.definition: Calculates the fraction of a year represented by the whole days between start_date and end_date.
semantics.argument_truncation: Microsoft specifies that all arguments are truncated to integers; this evaluator truncates toward zero before range and basis checks.
semantics.actual_days: Bases 2 and 3 divide the signed whole-serial-day difference by 360 and 365 respectively.
semantics.actual_actual_profile: Basis 1 splits the signed interval at Excel calendar-year boundaries and sums each segment divided by that calendar year length (365 or 366, with Excel serial year 1900 treated as 366). Microsoft names the basis and documents a leap-year example but does not specify this multi-year algorithm; it is an evaluator profile inspired by day-count structure, not a verified Excel claim.
semantics.signed_reverse_profile: Reversed intervals return a signed negative fraction. Microsoft does not specify the sign behavior on the function page; this remains an evaluator profile.
semantics.february_warning: Microsoft warns that the US (NASD) basis may return an incorrect result when start_date is the last day of February.
semantics.invalid_date: Invalid start_date or end_date returns #VALUE!, as Microsoft documents; supported numeric serials are 0 through 2958465.
semantics.invalid_basis: A basis below 0 or above 4 returns #NUM!, as Microsoft documents, after integer truncation.
semantics.fractional_serial_profile: All arguments are truncated toward zero per Microsoft; locale-dependent text-date parsing is unsupported.
semantics.serial_60: Preserves Excel compatibility serial 60 in actual-day subtraction and uses a 366-day evaluator year for 1900; exact Excel behavior around serial 60 is unverified.
semantics.date_system: Assumes the 1900 date system; workbook-specific 1904 dates are not modeled.

semantics.documented_behavior: Returns value_if_true when logical_test is TRUE and value_if_false when it is FALSE; Microsoft documents the third argument as optional.
semantics.default: An omitted optional value_if_false returns FALSE in the Workbook Forge profile.
semantics.evaluation_profile: Workbook Forge evaluates only the selected result branch. Microsoft documents branch selection but does not specify the evaluator error-order contract.
semantics.explicit_omission_profile: An explicitly empty selected branch returns #VALUE! in Workbook Forge. Microsoft examples and problem notes differ on empty branch slots; this profile has not been checked directly in Excel.
semantics.array_result_profile: A selected generated array preserves its shape through evaluate_result. This formula result is not projected into worksheet spill cells.

semantics.documented_behavior: Returns value_if_error when value evaluates to a supported error; otherwise returns the formula result.
semantics.documented_array_behavior: Microsoft documents element-wise array results for array formulas. Workbook Forge currently passes a generated array through as one shaped result and does not apply value_if_error element-wise to error cells inside arrays or ranges.
semantics.array_result_profile: A selected generated array or array fallback preserves shape through evaluate_result. Worksheet spill placement is unsupported.

semantics.documented_behavior: Returns value_if_na when value evaluates to #N/A; otherwise returns the formula result.
semantics.error_scope: Catches #N/A only; other supported errors are preserved.
semantics.array_result_profile: A selected generated array or array fallback preserves shape through evaluate_result. The current evaluator does not apply value_if_na element-wise to #N/A cells inside arrays or ranges, and does not project worksheet spills.

semantics.definition: Joins text from multiple values, ranges, or arrays into one text result.
semantics.argument_limit: Accepts up to 253 text arguments; each argument may be a string or an array/range.
semantics.flattening_profile: The evaluator flattens supplied ranges and arrays in row-major order into one scalar result.
semantics.error_profile: Both evaluators propagate an encountered formula error before converting it to text. This local CONCAT profile is informed by Microsoft guidance for the superseded CONCATENATE function and has not been checked directly in Excel.
semantics.numeric_to_text_profile: Microsoft says combined numbers use the underlying value rather than the cell display format and recommends TEXT when explicit formatting is needed. The cited documentation does not specify exact default rendering. Workbook Forge uses a shared shortest round-tripping decimal representation: integer-valued numbers have no decimal suffix, negative zero is rendered as 0, and scientific notation uses lowercase e with at least two exponent digits. Finite Python integer inputs are rounded to binary64 before rendering to match Rust; an integer that cannot be represented as a finite binary64 value returns #NUM! in both evaluators. This formatting profile has not been checked directly in Excel.
semantics.result_limit: A result over 32,767 UTF-16 code units returns #VALUE!; the unit counting is the evaluator profile used to enforce Excel’s documented 32,767-character cell limit.
semantics.compatibility_limit: Returns a scalar string and does not use cell number formats or project dynamic-array results into worksheet cells.
